PHSCS 587

MOS body effect

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how depletion charge makes threshold voltage depend on source-to-body bias

For an nMOS in a p-type body, define VSB = VS − VB. Increasing a nonnegative VSB reverse biases the source–body junction, enlarges depletion charge and requires a larger gate voltage to establish inversion.

A uniform-doping approximation is Vth = Vth0 + γ[√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)], with γ = √(2qεsiNA)/Cₒₓ. Here φF = UT ln(NA/nᵢ) is positive for the chosen p-body convention, Cₒₓ is per area, and γ has units √V.

Signs matter. A formula written with VBS instead uses VBS = −VSB. The expression assumes depletion electrostatics, adequate ionization and reverse bias. It should not be extrapolated into forward-junction conduction.

Example

With γ = 0.45 √V, 2φF = 0.70 V and VSB = 0.90 V, threshold rises by about 0.193 V relative to the zero-body-bias value.

Practice

1. If the body voltage falls while source voltage stays fixed, what happens to nMOS threshold in this model?

First determine the sign of the change in VSB.

VSB increases, depletion charge increases and threshold rises, provided the source–body junction remains reverse biased.
